newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel industry leader calls for more budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: Israel industry leader calls for more budget cuts.

text.p: The president of Israel's Manufacturers Association on Thursday called on the government to cut an additional one billion shekels from the 1997 budget.
Speaking at the association's annual meeting, Dan Propper said the government should implement the additional cut by reducing the number of public sector employees.
The government in October will submit to parliament a proposal to cut 4.9 billion shekels, or 3.2 percent of the 1997 budget, excluding debt servicing.
Propper said lax fiscal policy was partly to blame for an expected slowdown in economic growth.
"The slowdown that is expected....began with public sector wage increases, reached a peak with a loosening of the belt in 1995 and has now worsened because of a decrease in revenues," Propper said.

Finance Minister Dan Meridor noted that real wages in the public sector grew 25 percent in the past three to four years. He said public sector workers should not expect any increases in real wages at this point and urged the private sector to also exercise restraint.
Propper also said the Bank of Israel's tight monetary policy was hurting the economy. High interest rates had led to an overvalued shekel, which had hurt industry and exports, he said.
"The shekel exchange rate is now 10 percent below what it should be, if considering an inflation of 12 percent," Propper said. Inflation is forecast at 12 percent this year.
But Propper said underlying inflation was closer to 17 percent.
He called on the Bank of Israel "to get down from its ladder of stubbornness".
He said Israel could be headed for a recession or an economic crisis similar to one in Mexico, where a sharp devaluation of the peso sparked a flight of capital.
Propper said a balanced policy was needed, including steeper budget cuts, a reduction in interest rates and measures to stimulate growth and privatisation.
If that was not possible, the government should at least lower interest rates to depreciate the shekel, even though this would likely lead to a two or three percent rise in inflation, he said.
